name: Frieda Krueger

inspiration.oldScript: The boogeyman as a child-killer in a striped sweater, and Freddy's Revenge (1985), whose monster doubled as a gay-panic metaphor for a boy's desire.
inspiration.newLens: A woman stylist lied out of town by a moral-panic PTA for letting kids look like themselves. Her rage is real but aimed at the wrong generation, and the cure is the truth.

logline: Fall asleep on Crystal Street and Frieda will be happy to give you a little off the top. Wherever she cuts, your color drains to gray.
backstory: In 1961 Frieda Krueger ran the Shear Delight salon at the end of the Glimmer Falls shopping plaza. Every bride, prom queen and church soloist in town sat in her chair, and she gave the girls nobody else would touch their first pixie cuts, mohawks and dyed-blue bobs. When the founding PTA mothers decided her salon was "a bad influence," one of them started a rumor that Frieda was poisoning hair dye. The plaza owners evicted her by Christmas. Frieda kept cutting hair in her basement until the night the boiler went out and she fell asleep in her own chair and never woke up. Now she cuts in dreams, with a glove of five polished shears, and she is determined to make the children of those mothers perfect: neat, gray and exactly alike.

centralIssue.title: The rumor that made her a monster
centralIssue.summary: Frieda was not a poisoner. Someone lied her out of town for letting kids look like themselves. Her rage is real, but it is aimed at the wrong generation. Uncover who started the rumor and help her be seen as the artist she was.

poster: A towering woman in a 1961 beautician's smock and a beehive of silver hair, a glove of five gleaming shears raised over a sleeping suburban street, curlers floating like moons, the houses below draining from color to gray
portrait: Close portrait of a sharp-cheeked 1960s beautician ghost, silver beehive, cat-eye glasses with cracked lenses, a glove of five shears held near her face, half her face lit hot pink by a salon mirror
endingPhoto: A tall woman in a pink 1961 beautician's smock and a towering silver beehive leaning over a sleeping teenager's bed, her glove of five gleaming salon shears snipping a curl of dream-smoke, rows of hooded salon dryers looming like tombstones in a bedroom that melts into a midnight beauty parlor, pajama-clad friends bursting through the bedroom door behind her
taunts: Sit still, sugar. Perfect takes time.
Your mother had this exact cowlick. I fixed hers, too.
Gray is very in this season. Everyone will be wearing it.
Nobody ever leaves my chair unhappy. Nobody ever leaves.

clues.title: The eviction notice
clues.hint: The library keeps the Glimmer Falls Gazette on microfiche back to 1959.

encounter.title: Reel 1961-12
encounter.place: Microfiche room, Glimmer Falls Public Library
encounter.text: The microfiche reader hums like a refrigerator. December 1961 is missing from the drawer, but the reshelving cart has a reel labeled in someone's tidy script: DO NOT CIRCULATE. Ms. Hart is busy at the front desk, and the reel is still warm, as if someone was just reading it.
encounter.art: A teenager in a dim library microfiche room, a glowing green reader screen showing a 1961 newspaper headline about a salon eviction, a reel with a stern red restricted label

choices.label: Thread the forbidden reel and read fast

success.text: SHEAR DELIGHT CLOSED AFTER 'DYE SCARE,' reads the headline. No test ever found poison. The only source quoted is an unnamed PTA officer. You print the page before the reel snaps.
success.art: A printed microfiche page sliding out of a library printer, headline about a dye scare, a hand-drawn heart circling the key line of the article

failure.text: The reel spins loose and clatters across the floor. When you look up, the reader screen shows your own reflection with gray hair, smiling with somebody else's lipstick. The lights flicker and the reel is gone.
failure.art: A library microfiche screen showing a teenager's reflection with gray hair and a stranger's red smile, a film reel unspooling across the carpet

choices.label: Ask Ms. Hart why this reel is restricted

success.text: Ms. Hart lowers her glasses. "Because the woman who started that rumor sits on the library board." She lets you read the article in her office, then tucks a photocopy into a book jacket so it looks like homework.
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan sliding a photocopied newspaper inside a hardcover book jacket across a desk to a teenager, warm lamp light

failure.text: Ms. Hart says the reel is "being repaired" in a voice that means a grown-up has told her to say that. On your way out you notice a library board photo on the wall. One woman's face has been scratched out with something very sharp.
failure.art: A framed library board photograph in a hallway with one woman's face scratched out by five parallel blade marks

clues.title: Frieda's portfolio
clues.hint: Somebody at the Glitter Box Playhouse has been doing wigs since the sixties.

encounter.title: The wig room
encounter.text: Glory Hallelujah's wig room is a wall of foam heads, each with a name: Cher, Dusty, Big Sandy, Miss Frieda. That last one wears a towering silver beehive, and under it, taped to the foam, is an old photo album bursting with Polaroids of kids in impossible haircuts, all of them grinning.
encounter.art: A backstage wig room lined with foam mannequin heads wearing sparkling wigs, one silver beehive labeled Miss Frieda, an old photo album open beneath it full of 1960s haircut snapshots

choices.label: Ask Glory who Miss Frieda was

success.text: Glory sits down hard. "She cut my hair when I was nine, the first time anyone let me look how I felt inside. Lost her shop over a lie." She hands you the album. Every page is signed: You're perfect already. Love, F.
success.art: A drag queen in a feathered robe sitting at a vanity mirror, holding an old photo album to her chest, tearful and smiling, bulb lights glowing

failure.text: Glory is mid-rehearsal and waves you off with a fan. When you reach for the album, the beehive wig turns on its foam head to face you. You leave very quickly.
failure.art: A silver beehive wig on a foam mannequin head turned toward the viewer in a dark backstage room, one curler dropping to the floor

choices.label: Snap the album pages before anyone notices

success.text: Click, whirr, click. Twelve Polaroids develop in your pocket: a boy with a lightning-bolt part, twin girls with matching blue bobs, a kid in a tiara who looks a lot like a young Glory. Frieda made people brave.
success.art: A spread of fresh Polaroid photos on a backstage floor showing 1960s kids with bold, joyful haircuts, a camera beside them

failure.text: The flash goes off in a mirror and the whole wig wall is lit up. Frankie catches you, sighs, and makes you sweep the stage. By the time you finish, the album is locked in Glory's trunk.
failure.art: A teenager sweeping a glittery stage under a single work light while a stage manager in headphones watches with arms crossed

clues.title: Mrs. Whitlock's confession
clues.hint: The oldest house on Crystal Street belongs to a founding PTA mother who never sleeps anymore.

encounter.title: The woman who never sleeps
encounter.text: Old Mrs. Whitlock sits on her porch at noon in a quilted robe, a pot of coffee at her elbow and every light in her house on. Her hair is perfectly, uniformly gray. "I haven't slept in twenty-five years," she says, before you ask anything at all.
encounter.art: An elderly suburban woman in a quilted robe on a porch at noon, every window of her split-level house lit, a coffee pot beside her, hair perfectly gray, purple shadows under her eyes

choices.label: Sit down and pour her another cup

success.text: Over the second pot she tells you. She started the rumor because Frieda gave her daughter a pixie cut and the other mothers laughed at her. "I was jealous and cruel," she whispers. "Tell her I'm sorry, if you see her. I see her every time I blink."
success.art: A teenager and an elderly woman sharing coffee on a porch swing, the woman weeping into a handkerchief, a faded photo of a girl with a pixie cut between them

failure.text: She gets defensive, then frightened, then furious, and calls your parents to report you for loitering. Behind her, in the dark front window, a gloved hand with five shears taps the glass in rhythm.
failure.art: A dark front window of a suburban house, a glove of five shears tapping the glass from inside, an old woman on the porch shouting into a cordless phone

choices.label: Lay out what you know and make her admit it

success.text: You list the dates, the missing reel, the scratched photo. Her coffee cup rattles. "Yes. It was me. I said the dye was poison and they believed me because I was the sort of woman people believed." She signs a note you can carry: I LIED. I'M SORRY. — J.W.
success.art: A shaking elderly hand signing an apology note on a porch table beside a coffee cup, a teenager standing firm, late afternoon light

failure.text: She laughs at you, a brittle, practiced laugh, and goes inside. Every light in her house goes out at once. For the first time in twenty-five years, Mrs. Whitlock is asleep, and the whole street hears her scream.
failure.art: A split-level house on a cul-de-sac with every light suddenly out, a single scream line drawn in the air above it, neighbors' porch lights flicking on

signature.title: The Chair
signature.place: The Shear Delight salon, in a dream
signature.text: You do not remember falling asleep. You are in a pink vinyl salon chair, the cape snapped at your throat, and in the mirror a woman with a silver beehive is combing your hair with one shear-blade fingernail. "Just a trim," Frieda says. "Something sensible. Something gray."
signature.art: A teenager trapped in a pink vinyl salon chair in a dreamy, warped 1961 beauty parlor, a ghostly beautician with a five-shear glove looming in the mirror, hair dryers hanging like moons

choices.label: Pinch yourself awake before she cuts

success.text: You twist the skin on your wrist until the salon smears like wet paint. You jolt upright in bed, the cape still around your neck, a single silver curler on your pillow. You are wide awake and very, very alive.
success.art: A teenager bolting upright in a 1980s bedroom with posters on the walls, a salon cape still around their neck, a silver curler on the pillow

failure.text: Snip. A lock of your hair falls into your lap, gray as cigarette ash. When you wake, that streak is still gray, and you feel a little more tired than you did before.
failure.art: A single gray lock of hair falling onto a pink salon cape, a reflection of shears flashing in a mirror

choices.label: Ask for her best cut, the one nobody else would dare

success.text: Frieda's shears stop. In the mirror, something like delight crosses her face. "Nobody has asked me that in twenty-five years." She gives you a cut so fierce it survives waking up, and then she lets you go.
success.art: A teenager in a salon chair with a fierce, glittering, rainbow-streaked haircut, a ghostly beautician behind them almost smiling in the mirror

failure.text: "Dare?" She laughs. "Darling, I tried daring. Look where it got me." The chair spins and spins and you wake on the floor of your room, dizzy, with a crown of curlers tangled in your hair.
failure.art: A dizzy teenager waking on a bedroom carpet tangled in pink foam curlers, a spinning salon chair fading into the wallpaper

signature.title: The Gray Street
signature.text: Crystal Street is perfectly gray. The lawns, the station wagons, the neighbors standing on every porch in matching gray bathrobes and matching gray bobs. They turn their heads toward you all at once. "Your turn," they say, in your neighbors' voices.
signature.art: A 1980s suburban cul-de-sac drained entirely of color, neighbors in identical gray bathrobes and identical gray haircuts on every porch turning toward one colorful teenager in the street

choices.label: Run for the one house still in color

success.text: Your sneakers slap gray asphalt. Grandma Pearl's porch light is still yellow, and you dive through it like a finish line. Inside, everything is warm and loud and real, and you wake up laughing.
success.art: A teenager diving through a glowing yellow porch light into a warm, colorful living room while a gray suburban street reaches after them

failure.text: The neighbors move without walking, like a slide show. Every time you blink they are closer. When you wake, your favorite jacket is gray, and so is the poster above your bed.
failure.art: Gray-robed neighbors frozen mid-step much closer than before, like slides in a slideshow, surrounding a frightened teenager on a gray street

choices.label: Pull out a lipstick and start drawing color back

success.text: You draw a hot pink star on the asphalt and it blazes. Then a turquoise lightning bolt, a purple heart. Color spreads in rings and the neighbors blink like people waking from a long, dull dream.
success.art: A teenager drawing glowing neon pink stars and turquoise lightning bolts on gray asphalt with a lipstick, color spreading outward across a suburban street

failure.text: The lipstick comes out gray. Everything you draw comes out gray. A gloved hand rests gently on your shoulder, and you wake with five neat, bloodless lines in your pajama sleeve.
failure.art: A gray lipstick star smeared on gray asphalt, a glove of shears resting on a teenager's shoulder from behind

signature.title: One, Two, Frieda's Coming
signature.place: The Crystal Street sidewalk, in a dream, at a dusk that never ends
signature.text: It is dusk on Crystal Street, and it has been dusk for hours. Under the streetlight, three little girls in matching gray pinafores and matching gray bobs are jumping rope, and the rope makes a sound like scissors closing. "One, two, Frieda's coming for you," they chant. "Three, four, sweep the salon floor. Five, six, bobby pins and picks." On seven, all three of them turn and say your name.
signature.art: Three little girls in matching gray pinafores and gray bob haircuts jumping rope under a streetlight on a dreamlike suburban street at an endless violet dusk, a teenager watching from the sidewalk, bobby pins glinting on the pavement

choices.label: Jump in and change the rhyme

success.text: You jump into the middle and chant right over them: "Seven, eight, Frieda's cuts were great! Nine, ten, do my hair again!" The rope stumbles. The girls giggle, real giggles, and their pinafores bloom pink and yellow and blue. You wake up still chanting, feet tangled in the sheets, with a grin you cannot explain at breakfast.
success.art: A teenager jumping rope between three giggling little girls under a streetlight on a dreamlike suburban street at dusk, the girls' gray pinafores blooming into pink, yellow and blue, the rope swinging in a bright arc

failure.text: The rope catches your ankle like a telephone cord and wraps, and wraps. The chant gets faster. You wake on your bedroom floor rolled up in your own bedsheet, and the whole room smells like perm solution.
failure.art: A teenager waking on a bedroom carpet tightly rolled in a twisted bedsheet, a gray jump rope looped around one ankle, faint ghostly bobby pins scattered across the floor

choices.label: Step in and catch the rope mid-swing

success.text: You plant your feet and catch the rope in both fists. It bucks like a garden hose, then goes slack. The girls scatter like pigeons, leaving bobby pins rolling in the gutter, and the streetlight finally clicks over from dusk to night. Night means you can wake up, so you do.
success.art: A teenager gripping a slack jump rope in both fists under a streetlight on a dusky suburban street, three gray-clad little girls scattering away, bobby pins rolling along the gutter

failure.text: The rope keeps turning and lifts you right off your feet. You skip, and skip, and skip, chanting along against your will, until your calves burn and dawn finally drags you out of the dream. Your legs ache all through first period.
failure.art: A teenager lifted off the ground mid-skip inside a whirling gray jump rope under a streetlight, three gray-bobbed little girls turning it with eerie smiles, a dreamy violet sky overhead

choices.label: Count ahead in the rhyme and wake yourself on ten

success.text: Every jump-rope rhyme ends on ten, and you can hear where this one lands: never sleep again. On nine you bite your tongue, hard. On ten you are sitting up in bed, wide awake, while the last word dies in your ears. You write the whole rhyme down before you can forget it.
success.art: A teenager sitting bolt upright in a 1980s bedroom at night scribbling in a spiral notebook by flashlight, faint ghostly jump-rope girls fading into the flowered wallpaper behind them

failure.text: The rhyme does not end at ten. "Eleven, twelve," the girls chant, and then your name, and then your street address. You wake at exactly three a.m., certain that Frieda has just written you into her appointment book.
failure.art: A teenager waking in a dark bedroom staring at a glowing red alarm clock, the shadow of a swinging jump rope sweeping across the wall, three small silhouettes standing outside the window

signature.title: The Rinse
signature.text: You are rinsing shampoo out of your hair at the bathroom sink, eyes squeezed shut, so tired you are swaying. The water gets warmer. The sink gets deeper. When you crack one eye, the basin has become a black porcelain salon shampoo bowl, the faucet a chrome sprayer, and someone behind you is humming the old Shear Delight radio jingle. Up out of the suds beside your ear rise five polished shears, like the fin of a shark.
signature.art: A sleepy teenager bent over a bathroom sink at night with shampoo in their hair, the basin transformed into a deep black porcelain salon shampoo bowl, five polished shear blades rising out of the suds like a shark fin

choices.label: Jerk upright and slam the medicine cabinet in her face

success.text: You whip your head up, dripping, and see her in the medicine-cabinet mirror: silver beehive, shear glove raised. You slam the cabinet so hard the toothbrush cup jumps. When you open it again there is only your own wet, furious face, and from the drain comes a small, offended voice: "Well!"
success.art: A dripping teenager slamming a medicine cabinet shut in a 1980s bathroom, a ghostly silver beehive and a five-shear glove vanishing in the mirror, a toothbrush cup leaping off the sink

failure.text: The suds pull, warm and heavy, and you slide down into a dream salon. You wake on the bath mat with your hair set in a stiff 1961 bouffant that will not come down for anything: water, a comb, a whole can of Aqua-Glow. You wear it to school. People stare.
failure.art: A mortified teenager in a school hallway with a towering stiff 1961 bouffant hairdo, classmates staring from open lockers, a can of hairspray clutched in one hand

choices.label: Ask for the full treatment: deep condition, hot towel, the works

success.text: The humming stops. "Finally," Frieda sighs, "someone with standards." She works conditioner into your scalp with surprising tenderness, talking the whole time about a skinny kid from the Glitter Box who sat in her chair every Saturday, and the girls nobody else would touch. You wake with the softest hair of your life and the feeling you were told something important.
success.art: A relaxed teenager tipped back at a dreamy 1961 salon shampoo bowl, a ghostly beautician with a silver beehive gently massaging conditioner into their hair, soft pink light, steam curling from a hot towel

failure.text: "Hold still, you squirmy thing." She scrubs too hard, and the shears click closer with every pass. You jolt awake with soap in your eyes and five perfectly straight parts combed into your hair, neat as notebook paper.
failure.art: A teenager blinking soap from their eyes at a bathroom sink at night, five perfectly straight parts combed into their wet hair, a faint ghostly shear glove reflected in the steamy mirror

choices.label: Feel under the suds for the drain and pull the plug

success.text: Your fingers find the chain and yank. With an enormous glug the whole dream salon swirls down the drain, chairs, dryers, a shriek of outrage and all. On the porcelain afterward, glinting in a ring of suds, is a silver scrunchie that was definitely not there before.
success.art: A bathroom sink at night with a whirlpool of suds draining away, tiny ghostly salon chairs and hair dryers swirling down the drain, a silver scrunchie glinting on the wet porcelain rim

failure.text: The plug is a pink foam curler, and pulling it only makes the water rise. It fills the bowl, the bathroom, the dream, warm as a bath, while the shears circle you like a lazy fish. You wake on the tile at dawn, damp to the elbows, with the faucet still running.
failure.art: A teenager curled on bathroom tile at dawn, damp to the elbows, a faucet still running into an overflowing sink, a pink foam curler floating in the water

signature.title: Bring Something Back
signature.place: Frieda's basement, in a dream, one minute before your alarm
signature.text: You fall asleep on purpose, alarm set for three, clutching the old horror-movie rule: grab something in a dream and hold on, and you can bring it back. You land in a cold basement lit by one bare bulb, a salon chair bolted to the concrete beside a dead boiler, and shelves of foam wig heads with faces painted gray. Frieda sits at a card table with her back to you, writing in a pink appointment book. Your alarm will ring in one minute.
signature.art: A cold 1961 basement lit by a single bare bulb, a pink salon chair bolted to concrete beside an old boiler, shelves of foam wig heads painted gray, a beehived beautician at a card table writing in a pink appointment book

choices.label: Snatch the pink appointment book off the table

success.text: You snatch it and clutch it to your chest as Frieda spins around. The alarm shrieks, and you wake with your arms locked around a pink appointment book that smells of hairspray and boiler smoke. The last page is dated December 1961, and every booking after the eviction is a girl's name with the same note beside it: no charge.
success.art: A teenager waking in bed at night hugging a worn pink appointment book to their chest, an alarm clock jangling on the nightstand, a faint wisp of boiler smoke curling over the blankets

failure.text: Your fingers close on it and it turns to hair, a fistful of gray clippings that slither out of your grip. Frieda turns and smiles. "Don't touch the books, dear." The alarm rings, and you wake clutching a handful of gray lint.
failure.art: A teenager waking in bed clutching a fistful of gray hair clippings slipping through their fingers, an alarm clock ringing, the shadow of a beehive hairdo looming on the wall

choices.label: Lunge for the shear glove itself

success.text: You lunge and hook two fingers through the glove's knuckle loop just as the alarm goes off. You wake with a single polished shear clattering onto your pillow, cold and real. Frieda will be one blade short tonight, and you have proof that nobody on this street will believe.
success.art: A single polished silver shear blade lying on a pillow in a dark 1980s bedroom, a startled teenager sitting up beside it, an alarm clock mid-ring on the nightstand

failure.text: She is faster than you. The shears close on your sleeve and pin it to the card table while the alarm rings and rings in another world. When you finally wake, your pajama sleeve has been neatly scalloped like a doily, all the way to the elbow.
failure.art: A teenager in bed at dawn holding up a pajama sleeve cut into neat lacy scallops to the elbow, a ringing alarm clock, pale morning light through the blinds

choices.label: Ask her, politely, for one of her business cards

success.text: Frieda stares at you for a long moment. Then she opens a drawer and hands you a small pink card: SHEAR DELIGHT, PLAZA SUITE 4, WALK-INS WELCOME. "Nobody has asked for one since the plaza," she says quietly. You wake holding it, and it still smells faintly of roses.
success.art: A teenager waking in bed holding a small pink business card up to the moonlight, rose petals scattered on the blanket, a ghostly beehived silhouette fading into the wallpaper

failure.text: "A card?" She laughs. "Where would you even take it? They threw all mine in the dumpster with the dye." The bulb flares white, and you wake at three on the dot with a paper cut on your thumb and an empty hand.
failure.art: A teenager in a dark bedroom staring at a tiny paper cut on their thumb, an alarm clock glowing at the bedside, a bare basement bulb flaring in a dreamy haze above the bed

signature.title: Slumber Party Rules
signature.text: Your crew is camped on your living room floor in sleeping bags, swearing nobody will fall asleep. It is three a.m. One by one, heads are nodding. In the dark kitchen, very softly, someone is sharpening scissors.
signature.art: A 1980s living room slumber party at 3 a.m., teens in sleeping bags fighting sleep around a glowing TV, a silhouette in the dark kitchen sharpening scissors

choices.label: Start the loudest game of Truth or Dare in history

success.text: By dawn everyone knows who kissed who at the roller rink, Moose has confessed to knitting a sweater for his cat, and nobody slept a wink. The scissor sound stops at sunrise, sulking.
success.art: Teens laughing hysterically in sleeping bags at dawn, popcorn everywhere, sunlight through the blinds, a pair of scissors abandoned on the kitchen counter

failure.text: The game peters out. Someone starts snoring. You hear a snip, a gasp, and in the morning one friend has a perfect gray bowl cut and will not talk about what they saw.
failure.art: A morning living room after a slumber party, one teen with a perfect gray bowl cut staring blankly into space, friends gathered around worried

choices.label: Booby-trap the kitchen with every pot you own

success.text: At 3:33 the kitchen explodes in a crash of saucepans and a shriek of outrage. In the morning there is a silver beehive hairpin on the linoleum, and you feel, for the first time, that Frieda can be surprised.
success.art: A dark kitchen exploding in falling pots and pans, a startled ghostly beehive silhouette, a silver hairpin spinning on linoleum

failure.text: The pots fall on you, not her. By the time you dig yourself out, half the party is asleep and dreaming the same dream: a pink chair, waiting.
failure.art: A teenager buried under a pile of pots and pans in a dark kitchen while friends sleep behind them, a pink salon chair glowing faintly in a dream bubble

finale.title: Closing Time at the Shear Delight
finale.place: The Shear Delight salon, Halloween night
finale.text: On Halloween night the whole street falls asleep at once and you all wake up in the Shear Delight. Every neighbor is in a chair. Every chair faces a mirror. Frieda stands in the center with her shears raised, and for the first time you notice she is crying. "I only wanted them to be perfect," she says, "so nobody could take anything away from them."
finale.art: A vast dream beauty salon with endless rows of pink chairs holding sleeping neighbors, a weeping ghostly beautician with a raised five-shear glove at the center, the teen crew facing her in Halloween costumes

choices.label: Smash every mirror in the salon

success.text: Mirror after mirror bursts into glitter. With nowhere left to see herself, Frieda comes apart like smoke from a curling iron. The neighbors wake up in their own beds, a little grayer, a little shaken, and safe.
success.art: A teen swinging a baseball bat through a salon mirror that bursts into glittering shards, a beautician ghost dissolving into pink smoke

failure.text: The glass will not break. In every mirror, your reflection is getting a neat, sensible, gray haircut, and it looks so relieved.
failure.art: Endless salon mirrors each reflecting a teenager calmly receiving a gray haircut, the real teenager pounding unbroken glass

choices.label: Spin her own chair until she falls asleep inside her dream

success.text: You lure her into the pink chair, snap the cape around her and spin. A dream inside a dream is too deep even for a ghost. Frieda sleeps, finally, and the salon folds up around her like a closing compact.
success.art: A ghostly beautician spinning in her own pink salon chair, wrapped in a cape and falling asleep, the salon folding shut like a makeup compact

failure.text: She catches the chair with one shear-tipped hand. "Oh, sweetheart. I invented that trick." The cape snaps around your throat instead.
failure.art: A beautician ghost stopping a spinning salon chair with one bladed hand, a cape snapping around a teenager instead

choices.label: Show her the portfolio, the newspaper and the apology

success.text: You hold up the article that proved her innocent, the album full of brave kids, and the note: I LIED. I'M SORRY. Frieda reads it three times. Then she lowers the shears, takes off the glove finger by finger, and asks, very quietly, if anyone wants a real haircut.
success.art: A ghostly beautician removing a glove of shears finger by finger, reading an apology note, surrounded by teens holding up a photo album and a newspaper, color flooding back into the salon

failure.text: She cannot hear you over twenty-five years of anger. The salon tilts. You have the truth in your hands, but she needs to see it more clearly than this.
failure.art: A tilting dream salon, a teen holding up an apology note that a raging beautician ghost cannot see through a storm of hair clippings

best.title: You're Perfect Already
best.text: Frieda spends her last night on Crystal Street giving the most glorious haircuts in Glimmer Falls history: a purple mohawk for Moose, silver stars for Bea, something unrepeatable and rainbow for you. Mrs. Whitlock comes in last, and the two women talk for a long time with the door closed. At dawn the salon is empty except for a signed photo on the mirror: You're perfect already. Love, F. Every November after, someone leaves fresh curlers on the old plaza steps.
best.art: A joyful dream salon at dawn full of teens with wild rainbow haircuts, a softly glowing beautician ghost waving goodbye, a signed photo tucked in the mirror frame

good.title: Lights Out at the Salon
good.text: The Shear Delight goes dark for good and Crystal Street wakes up rested for the first time all week. Nobody remembers much, except a smell of hairspray and a vague feeling that they should be kinder to the strange kids. You remember. You keep a single silver curler on your desk, and sometimes you wonder what she was so afraid of.
good.art: A shuttered 1960s beauty salon at dawn with a closed sign, a teenager outside holding one silver curler, morning light on a quiet suburban plaza

bittersweet.title: A Little Off the Top
bittersweet.text: You survive the week, and so does most of Crystal Street, but a few neighbors wake up with gray in their hair that never washes out. Frieda is quiet now, not gone. On the coldest nights you still hear scissors, very far away, and you sleep with the radio on.
bittersweet.art: A teenager in bed with a clock radio glowing, a faint silhouette of shears in the frosty window, a gray streak in their hair

bad.title: Something Sensible
bad.text: You wake on November first with a neat gray haircut and no memory of the week. Your clothes are beige now. You like them. Your crew tries to remind you who you were, and you smile politely, and you sit perfectly still while they talk.
bad.art: A teenager with a neat gray haircut in beige clothes sitting perfectly still at a kitchen table, worried friends in colorful jackets crowded around them
